  - paragraph: The Record
  - heading "The last thing I got wrong is in here too." [level=2]

      - link "evidence":
        - /url: /accessibility/#receipts
      - time: 2026-08-25
  - paragraph: How the work gets made
  - heading "I direct AI agents, and I built the system that keeps them honest." [level=2]
  - paragraph: "The projects above were implemented by AI agents working inside a governance system I designed: fifteen roles with explicit domain boundaries, and a written constitution that outranks any individual role or prompt. The agents do the implementation, the tests, and most of the diagnosis. I set the problem, make the architectural calls, and gate what lands."
  - paragraph:
    - text: "The constraints are what make the output reviewable. Database migrations are files with a rollback, never applied changes: no agent applies one to production, or sends anything outside the repository, without my explicit authorization under a narrow, mechanically gated exception. None handles credentials. Exactly one of the fifteen may message me; the rest write to files I read on my own schedule. Merges to"
    - code: main
    - text: are mine, with one narrow gated exception I granted to a single project.
  - paragraph:
    - text: Here is the system working. An agent fixing something unrelated added two background-location permission strings to
    - code: app.json
    - text: ". The privacy role blocked it: the app uses no background-location APIs, so declaring them would invite an App Store 5.1.1 rejection and ask for a permission the product does not need. Both keys were removed; neither reached"
    - code: main
    - text: .
  - paragraph: And here is what it hands back. A review found that anonymous reports skipped a content filter that signed-in reports run. It was written up and deliberately left unpatched, because deciding what to filter on a submit form is a moderation policy, not a bug fix. It waited for me instead of being quietly patched, and the filter runs on both paths now.
  - paragraph: "The honest limit: these fences are prompt-level, not sandbox-level. It is one person’s system, tested across one person’s projects, and some of the governance overhead does not pay for itself."
  - paragraph: A Brief Account
  - heading "The work is careful. The record is honest." [level=2]
  - blockquote: One careful deliverable beats a dozen rough ones.
  - paragraph: Most of what I make starts with a problem worth solving. I prefer small, exact software to large, approximate software. I work from Canada, mostly on AI tooling, accessibility infrastructure, and the systems that make a product feel calm.
  - paragraph: I keep a written record of how each thing was made. The documentation is part of the deliverable, not an afterthought.

  - paragraph:
    - text: "Credentials, earned in order: 9 of them, with issuers and dates."
    - link "See the credential badges":

  - paragraph: Let’s talk

  - text: Skyler Halisky Technical Support AI-assisted Builder
  - paragraph: A Brief Account
  - heading "Support is the work and inspiration, building tools to solve problems and reduce friction." [level=1]
  - paragraph: I am Skyler Halisky.
  - paragraph: "By day, I’m a senior technical-support specialist: the escalation point for enterprise accounts, and I train and coach teammates. I came to software through problems I wanted to solve. Most of them involved accessibility: tools that should have been better but weren’t. I decided to make some that were."
  - blockquote: Accessibility is not an add-on. It is where you begin.
  - paragraph: I work from Canada. Mostly on AI-assisted tooling, accessibility infrastructure, and community software. I prefer learning in public.
  - paragraph: I keep a written record of how each thing was made. The documentation is part of the deliverable, not an afterthought.
  - paragraph: "Right now: an accessibility map. A multi-agent system that ships real commits. A local-first prompt manager. A command-line trainer. All of them documented in the open."
  - paragraph: Method
  - heading "How the work gets made is written down once." [level=2]
  - paragraph: "There is one account of my method on this site, and it is on the front page: the governance system the agents work inside, the constraints that make the output reviewable, a case where the system blocked something it should have, and the limit I have not solved."
  - paragraph: I would rather it exist once, accurately, than three times in three shortened forms.
  - link "Read how the work gets made":
    - /url: /#how-i-work
  - paragraph: Principles
  - heading "Accessibility. Privacy. No shortcuts." [level=2]
  - paragraph: Flagstone is built and tested against WCAG 2.2 AA, with the methods and limitations documented in its case study. Flagstone exists because disabled people deserve navigation tools designed for them, not adapted for them.
  - paragraph: "The user’s data is theirs. Prompt Library stores everything locally: no backend of mine, no account, no telemetry. Runs go directly from the browser to Anthropic with the user’s own key; nothing passes through a server I control. If the data is not necessary, do not collect it."
  - paragraph: I would rather take longer and do it correctly than ship fast and apologise. This is not a principle from a book. It came from shipping things that were not ready.
  - paragraph: Currently
  - heading "Learning in public. Shipping on purpose." [level=2]
  - paragraph: "I am not a trained software engineer. I came to coding through building: I had ideas I wanted to exist. That is still how this works."
  - paragraph: "Right now: TypeScript, React Native, and multi-agent systems that stay inside their rules when I am not watching. Each project teaches something the last one did not."
  - paragraph: "The work I am aimed at is senior technical and product support: escalation, support tooling, support operations. Adjacent to it, and evidenced by the projects above: QA, accessibility, and privacy-aware systems work."

  - heading "Accessibility is where I begin." [level=1]

  - article "Accessibility statement":
    - paragraph: "This site is built to be used by everyone, including people who navigate with a keyboard, a screen reader, or with motion turned down. This page is the honest record of that work: what I deliberately built in, and what I have not yet done. I would rather tell you exactly where it stands than claim a finish line I have not crossed."
    - heading "The standard I aim for" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: I build to
      - strong: WCAG 2.2 Level AA
      - text: ". To be clear about that word: this site has not been through a formal third-party audit, and nothing here is certified. AA is the bar I design and build against, not a badge I have been given. The specific choices below are real, and you can check them yourself."
    - heading "What I built in" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Keyboard, end to end.
      - text: "A “Skip to main content” link is the first thing on the page: hidden until you focus it, then it jumps you past the navigation to the main region. Every control is reachable by keyboard, and the mobile menu is a proper dialog: it keeps focus inside while it is open, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the button that opened it."
    - paragraph:
      - strong: A focus ring you can actually see.
      - text: "Move through the page by keyboard and the focused element gets a 2px terracotta outline that traces its own shape: pills stay pill-shaped, cards keep their corners. It clears the contrast WCAG asks of a focus indicator, in both the light and dark themes."
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Readable text in both themes.
      - text: Every text role (body, captions, links) meets WCAG AA contrast against its background, in light mode and dark mode alike.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Real structure underneath.
      - text: The page is built from honest landmarks (navigation, main, footer) in a sensible reading order, with a heading hierarchy a screen reader can move through. Links that open a new tab say so.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Motion that respects your settings.
      - text: "If your system asks for reduced motion, this site listens. The entrance animations, the scroll-linked day-to-night background, the page transitions, the small parallax: all of it holds still and shows you the finished, readable state instead of moving. A site-wide rule backs this up, so nothing decorative can slip past it."
    - paragraph: "You’re reading this because your system asked for less motion. The site listened: everything is already in place."
    - heading "Measured, not claimed" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Real numbers from a real run: measured"
      - time: 2026-08-25
      - text: ", method below. Not a live gate yet; a snapshot you can re-run."

    - heading "What I have not done" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "In the spirit of being honest about what ships:"
    - paragraph:
      - strong: No formal audit.
      - text: Conformance here is self-assessed against my own code, not certified by a third party, and not validated end to end with assistive technology across every browser and screen reader. I have not run a full manual screen-reader pass on this site. If you rely on one, I would genuinely like to hear how it goes.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The moving background is decorative.
      - text: The day-to-night world that shifts as you scroll is marked as decorative and hidden from screen readers. It carries no information you would miss, and it holds still under reduced motion. It is the one piece of visual flourish here, and I would rather name it than pretend the page is plain.
    - heading "Found a barrier? Tell me." [level=2]
    - paragraph: Accessibility barriers feel lonely when you face them alone. If something here got in your way (a control you could not reach, text you could not read, anything at all), I want to know. Tell me what broke and what you were trying to do. I read every message that comes through, and I will fix it.

- main:
  - text: Skyler Halisky Technical Support AI-assisted Builder
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":

        - link "Notes":

      - listitem: "Building Flagstone: A Lesson in Shipping Something That Matters"
  - time: May 29, 2026
  - text: 7 min read
  - 'heading "Building Flagstone: A Lesson in Shipping Something That Matters" [level=1]'
  - paragraph: "How I built a crowdsourced accessibility mapping app with Expo and Supabase: the technical decisions, the hard parts, and what actually shipped."
  - list "Tags":
    - listitem: accessibility
    - listitem: Expo
    - listitem: React Native
    - listitem: Supabase
  - 'article "Building Flagstone: A Lesson in Shipping Something That Matters"':
    - heading "The problem nobody was solving" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Accessibility infrastructure data is missing in most cities. Not wrong.
      - emphasis: Missing
      - text: ". If you use a wheelchair, a walker, or a guide cane, you already know this: you can look up whether a restaurant takes reservations, but you can’t reliably find out whether it has a step at the door."
    - paragraph: "The data that does exist is scattered. City governments sometimes publish ADA compliance records, but they’re PDFs from 2009. Google Maps has wheelchair-accessible icons, but they’re crowdsourced in ways users can’t easily contribute to or dispute. The result is a gap that falls hardest on the people with the least margin for a surprise: someone who can’t just “take the other entrance” when the main one turns out to have a broken ramp."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Flagstone is a mobile app that puts this data collection in users’ hands. Anyone can drop a flag on the map: a broken ramp, missing tactile paving, an entrance with an unmarked step, and the community can verify or dispute it. Verified flags persist. Disputed ones get reviewed. The goal is a living, ground-truth layer on top of the map that people can actually trust"
      - emphasis: before
      - text: they leave the house.
    - heading "Why Expo and Supabase" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: I could have built a web app. I didn’t, because the use case is fundamentally
      - emphasis: in the field
      - text: . You’re at the top of a hill wondering if the pharmacy three blocks down has a step at the entrance. You need a phone in your pocket and a notification when someone near you flags something. A Progressive Web App could technically handle this, but push notifications, deep offline support, and native map performance are all significantly smoother in a real native client.
    - paragraph: Expo lets me write React Native with one codebase and ship to both iOS and Android without maintaining two sets of native modules. That matters a lot for a solo project. The managed workflow handled 90% of the native complexity, including camera access, location permissions, and push tokens, without me touching Xcode or Android Studio configuration for most of the build.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Supabase was the natural backend choice for a few reasons. The Postgres row-level security model fits a user-contribution app well:"
      - code: auth.uid()
      - text: in RLS policies means users can only mutate their own flags without any application-layer enforcement code. The realtime subscription layer, a Postgres logical replication stream surfaced through Supabase’s WebSocket API, meant I could show new flags appearing on other users’ maps instantly, without polling. And the Supabase client handles auth tokens, refresh cycles, and session persistence in a way that works reliably against React Native’s AsyncStorage.
    - heading "The thing that was actually hard" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Making the interactive map work for screen reader users was the challenge I underestimated most.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The map component, rendered via
      - code: react-native-maps
      - text: ", is a single native view from the screen reader’s perspective. VoiceOver and TalkBack can’t enumerate individual flag markers as discrete accessible elements unless you do explicit work to expose them. The naive implementation produces an app where sighted users get a rich, interactive map with colored markers and a heatmap overlay, and screen reader users get one unlabeled blob."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The solution: a parallel accessibility layer. An invisible"
      - code: FlatList
      - text: positioned off-screen mirrors every visible flag as an accessible element with a proper label (“Broken ramp at Main St and 5th Ave, reported 3 days ago, verified by 2 people”). When a screen reader is active, this list is exposed and the map gets
      - code: accessibilityElementsHidden
      - text: . When it’s off, the list is hidden. It’s not perfect. The spatial relationship between flags is lost, but it gives screen reader users the actual data in navigable form rather than silence.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The EXIF privacy issue was a close second. When users attach photos to flags, the JPEG metadata can contain GPS coordinates precise enough to identify someone’s home if they’re reporting an inaccessible entrance nearby. Before any photo uploads to Supabase Storage, it goes through
      - code: expo-image-manipulator
      - text: to re-encode without metadata. Image quality is preserved; the coordinates are stripped. This runs on-device before the upload request fires, so the server never receives the EXIF data at all.
    - heading "What shipped" [level=2]
    - 'figure "What shipped: the interactive map, with a peer-verified, severity-graded barrier flag."':
      - img "Flagstone's map with a peer-verified severity-4 'No ramp' barrier flagged at a downtown Kelowna corner"
      - text: "What shipped: the interactive map, with a peer-verified, severity-graded barrier flag."
    - paragraph: The v1 TestFlight build at the time included the full core loop.
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: Interactive map
        - text: with clustering, color-coded flag markers (red for unverified, green for verified, gray for disputed), and a heatmap density overlay toggled from the toolbar.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Flag creation flow
        - text: ": drop a pin, choose a category, write a description, optionally attach a photo. Photos are EXIF-stripped on-device. Posted flags appear in realtime on other users’ maps via Supabase subscriptions."
      - listitem:
        - strong: Verification and dispute
        - text: "on any flag: two verifications push it to green; a net negative dispute score moves it to gray for review."
      - listitem:
        - strong: Push notifications
        - text: when a flag you submitted gets its first verification or reaches the verified threshold.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Offline-first flag browsing
        - text: ": flags for your current region are cached on-device. You can browse and read detail views without a connection; posting requires one."
      - listitem:
        - strong: WCAG 2.2 AA accessible UI
        - text: "throughout: the parallel screen-reader layer on the map, 44px minimum touch targets, sufficient color contrast on all flag states, and full keyboard navigation on iPad."
      - listitem:
        - strong: Dark mode
        - text: ": full system theme support, with the map style switching between light and satellite views."
    - heading "What’s next" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Status as of
      - time: May 29, 2026
    - paragraph: TestFlight is live. One early build, in exactly one outside tester’s hands. App Store submission is the next step; nothing has been submitted yet.
    - paragraph: "After that: the feature my one tester asked for first is search (find flags by address rather than navigating the map), and my own next priority is a proper dispute resolution flow (right now disputed flags sit in gray indefinitely; there should be a community review process). The data model already supports both. It’s a UI problem."
    - paragraph: "Longer term: I want to export the flag dataset as open data: a public API that cities, accessibility advocates, or other apps could consume. That’s the version of this project that has real scale impact."
    - blockquote: The app is the seed; the dataset is the thing that might matter.

  - heading "Continue reading." [level=2]

      - img "Flagstone's Explore map with an expanded verified Steep grade report, a real barrier photograph, orange map pins, map controls, and bottom navigation."

      - text: Accessibility infrastructure data is missing in most cities. Not wrong.
      - emphasis: Missing
      - text: ". If you use a wheelchair, a walker, or a guide cane, you already know this: you can look up whether a restaurant takes reservations, but you can’t reliably find out whether it has a step at the door."
    - paragraph: "The data that does exist is scattered. City governments sometimes publish ADA compliance records, but they’re PDFs from 2009. Google Maps has wheelchair-accessible icons, but they’re crowdsourced in ways users can’t easily contribute to or dispute. The result is a gap that falls hardest on the people with the least margin for a surprise: someone who can’t just “take the other entrance” when the main one turns out to have a broken ramp."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Flagstone is a mobile app that puts this data collection in users’ hands. Anyone can drop a flag on the map: a broken ramp, missing tactile paving, an entrance with an unmarked step, and the community can verify or dispute it. Verified flags persist. Disputed ones get reviewed. The goal is a living, ground-truth layer on top of the map that people can actually trust"
      - emphasis: before
      - text: they leave the house.
    - heading "Why Expo and Supabase" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: I could have built a web app. I didn’t, because the use case is fundamentally
      - emphasis: in the field
      - text: . You’re at the top of a hill wondering if the pharmacy three blocks down has a step at the entrance. You need a phone in your pocket and a notification when someone near you flags something. A Progressive Web App could technically handle this, but push notifications, deep offline support, and native map performance are all significantly smoother in a real native client.
    - paragraph: Expo lets me write React Native with one codebase and ship to both iOS and Android without maintaining two sets of native modules. That matters a lot for a solo project. The managed workflow handled 90% of the native complexity, including camera access, location permissions, and push tokens, without me touching Xcode or Android Studio configuration for most of the build.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Supabase was the natural backend choice for a few reasons. The Postgres row-level security model fits a user-contribution app well:"
      - code: auth.uid()
      - text: in RLS policies means users can only mutate their own flags without any application-layer enforcement code. The realtime subscription layer, a Postgres logical replication stream surfaced through Supabase’s WebSocket API, meant I could show new flags appearing on other users’ maps instantly, without polling. And the Supabase client handles auth tokens, refresh cycles, and session persistence in a way that works reliably against React Native’s AsyncStorage.
    - heading "The thing that was actually hard" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Making the interactive map work for screen reader users was the challenge I underestimated most.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The map component, rendered via
      - code: react-native-maps
      - text: ", is a single native view from the screen reader’s perspective. VoiceOver and TalkBack can’t enumerate individual flag markers as discrete accessible elements unless you do explicit work to expose them. The naive implementation produces an app where sighted users get a rich, interactive map with colored markers and a heatmap overlay, and screen reader users get one unlabeled blob."

      - code: FlatList

      - code: accessibilityElementsHidden
      - text: . When it’s off, the list is hidden. It’s not perfect. The spatial relationship between flags is lost, but it gives screen reader users the actual data in navigable form rather than silence.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The EXIF privacy issue was a close second. When users attach photos to flags, the JPEG metadata can contain GPS coordinates precise enough to identify someone’s home if they’re reporting an inaccessible entrance nearby. Before any photo uploads to Supabase Storage, it goes through
      - code: expo-image-manipulator
      - text: to re-encode without metadata. Image quality is preserved; the coordinates are stripped. This runs on-device before the upload request fires, so the server never receives the EXIF data at all.

    - paragraph: "Longer term: I want to export the flag dataset as open data: a public API that cities, accessibility advocates, or other apps could consume. That’s the version of this project that has real scale impact."

ariaSnapshot:
- link "Skip to main content":
  - /url: "#main"
- main:
  - text: Skyler Halisky Technical Support AI-assisted Builder
  - paragraph: Colophon
  - heading "How this was made." [level=1]
  - paragraph: The stack, the type, the world, and the quiet systems behind it.
  - article "Colophon":
    - paragraph: Most sites hide how they were made. This one tells you.
    - paragraph: "I keep a written record of how each thing was built: the documentation is part of the deliverable, not an afterthought. This page is that habit turned on the portfolio itself."
    - heading "The stack" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Most of this site is static. Next.js builds the public pages to plain HTML at compile time, so the portfolio itself runs no server, keeps no database, and asks nobody to sign in. There is one deliberate exception: a private, unlisted catalogue I keep for my own art, which signs in through Supabase and stores its records and photos there behind row-level security. It is not part of the public portfolio, and the rest of the site does not use it. React and TypeScript hold the structure; Tailwind handles the styling; Framer Motion and GSAP carry the motion. The words and the projects live in small JSON and Markdown files, checked by Zod every time the site builds: if the content is malformed, the build fails instead of shipping something broken. It is hosted on GitHub Pages, and once the checks pass, a change is live within a couple of minutes."
    - heading "The type" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Three typefaces, each with one job.
      - strong: Cormorant Garamond
      - text: "sets the serif crowns: the large titles that open each page."
      - strong: DM Sans
      - text: ", kept light, carries the body for calm reading."
      - strong: DM Mono
      - text: handles the small uppercase labels and the metadata. All three are self-hosted at build time, so reading this page makes no outside font requests.
    - heading "The world" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "The part you feel before you can name it: one continuous golden-hour desert that the whole site travels through. It opens at warm daylight and eases toward night as you scroll, cresting exactly as the footer arrives. Light mode is the daylight half of that world; dark mode is the night half: the same journey, told in each. It is decorative, hidden from screen readers, and it holds perfectly still the moment your system asks for reduced motion. The desert itself is generated: each vista begins in Midjourney, then I separate it by hand into the depth planes the scene travels through."
    - heading "The quiet systems" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A few details that repeat on purpose. The page titles wear an
      - strong: ember
      - text: "gradient: a warm rust-to-gold wash, with cool teal and moss variants so the warmth has something to lean on. Each project signs its own name with a"
      - strong: signature hue
      - text: "from the same golden-hour family (terracotta for Flagstone, phantom cyan for Ghost Code, gold for the Prompt Library) and sits in a frame true to its medium: a phone, a browser window, a clean plate. Even the numerals are deliberate: lined up while they count, old-style once they settle into prose."
    - heading "How it was made" [level=2]
    - paragraph: The same way everything here gets made. I describe the problem to Claude Code and build in the open, reading the output and correcting it when it goes wrong. For the larger work, a team of agents does the heavy lifting, each with a defined role and all of them working from a written constitution, so nothing is decided by accident. Nothing ships until I have used it. Then I write down what broke, and what the next person will need to know.
  - heading "The type, set live" [level=2]
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - paragraph: Built with intention
      - paragraph: Cormorant Garamond serif crowns
    - listitem:
      - paragraph: "Calm, readable body text: kept light so long-form never tires the eye."
      - paragraph: DM Sans body

      - paragraph: LABELS & METADATA
      - paragraph: DM Mono labels & metadata

  - navigation "Primary":

    - list:

  - heading "Accessibility" [level=1]
  - paragraph: An app about accessibility barriers has no business being one.
- group:
  - text: Display settings for this site ▸
  - paragraph: These change how this website looks and are remembered on this device. They don’t affect the Flagstone app itself — the app follows your phone’s own accessibility settings.
  - text: Text size
  - slider "Text size": "100"
  - text: Theme
  - group "Theme":
    - button "Dark"
    - button "High contrast"
  - text: Reading
  - group "Reading":
    - button "Spaced text"
    - button "Reduce motion"
  - button "Reset to defaults"
- status: Display settings reset to defaults
- main:
  - heading "Our commitment" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Flagstone exists so people can find out whether a place will work for them before they travel to it. The people who most need that answer are disabled people, so the app itself is built to be used with a screen reader, at large text sizes, with reduced motion, and without relying on colour to carry meaning. We target
    - strong: WCAG 2.2 Level AA
    - text: and Apple’s
    - link "iOS accessibility guidelines (opens in new tab)":
      - /url: https://developer.apple.com/accessibility/
    - text: .
  - heading "What the app supports" [level=2]
  - table "Accessibility features supported by the Flagstone iOS app":
    - caption: Accessibility features supported by the Flagstone iOS app
    - rowgroup:
      - row "Feature Status What that means here":
        - columnheader "Feature"
        - columnheader "Status"
        - columnheader "What that means here"
    - rowgroup:
      - row "VoiceOver Supported Every control has a spoken label, role, and where useful a hint. Status changes, filter results, and errors are announced. Photos carry descriptions written by the person who uploaded them.":
        - rowheader "VoiceOver"
        - cell "Supported"
        - cell "Every control has a spoken label, role, and where useful a hint. Status changes, filter results, and errors are announced. Photos carry descriptions written by the person who uploaded them."
      - row "Larger Text Supported Text scales with your Dynamic Type setting, including the accessibility sizes. Layouts reflow rather than clip.":
        - rowheader "Larger Text"
        - cell "Supported"
        - cell "Text scales with your Dynamic Type setting, including the accessibility sizes. Layouts reflow rather than clip."
      - row "Dark Interface Supported A full dark theme that follows your system setting, plus a manual toggle in Settings.":
        - rowheader "Dark Interface"
        - cell "Supported"
        - cell "A full dark theme that follows your system setting, plus a manual toggle in Settings."
      - row "Sufficient Contrast Supported Text and controls meet WCAG AA contrast ratios in both light and dark themes. Automated tests block changes that would regress this.":
        - rowheader "Sufficient Contrast"
        - cell "Supported"
        - cell "Text and controls meet WCAG AA contrast ratios in both light and dark themes. Automated tests block changes that would regress this."
      - row "Differentiate Without Colour Alone Supported Severity is shown as a number and a word, not just a colour. Status uses labelled badges. Links carry underlines.":
        - rowheader "Differentiate Without Colour Alone"
        - cell "Supported"
        - cell "Severity is shown as a number and a word, not just a colour. Status uses labelled badges. Links carry underlines."
      - row "Reduced Motion Supported When Reduce Motion is on, map and sheet animations are shortened or replaced with cross-fades.":
        - rowheader "Reduced Motion"
        - cell "Supported"
        - cell "When Reduce Motion is on, map and sheet animations are shortened or replaced with cross-fades."
      - row "Captions & Audio Descriptions Not applicable Flagstone contains no video or audio content, so there is nothing to caption or describe.":
        - rowheader "Captions & Audio Descriptions"
        - cell "Not applicable"
        - cell "Flagstone contains no video or audio content, so there is nothing to caption or describe."
      - row "Voice Control Under evaluation Controls are labelled in ways that should work with Voice Control, but we haven’t finished testing it end to end, so we don’t yet claim it.":
        - rowheader "Voice Control"
        - cell "Under evaluation"
        - cell "Controls are labelled in ways that should work with Voice Control, but we haven’t finished testing it end to end, so we don’t yet claim it."
  - heading "Designed for the way people actually use it" [level=2]
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - strong: You can browse without an account.
      - text: Reading the map, the part most people need, never requires signing up.
    - listitem:
      - strong: Touch targets are at least 44 × 44 points
      - text: ", the size Apple recommends for reliable tapping."
    - listitem:
      - strong: Reports say what they mean.
      - text: Severity carries a plain-language consequence, not just a number.
    - listitem:
      - strong: We never claim a place has no barriers.
      - text: We only say that nobody has reported one. An empty map means missing data, and the app says so.
    - listitem:
      - strong: Photos are optional and described.
      - text: A photo is never the only way information is conveyed.
  - heading "Known gaps" [level=2]
  - paragraph: "We would rather list these than pretend they don’t exist:"
  - list:
    - listitem: Voice Control has not been fully tested (see above).
    - listitem: Photo descriptions are optional, so older reports and reports from people who skipped the field may have no description beyond the barrier’s own text.
    - listitem: The map itself is inherently visual. We pair it with a text list of nearby barriers, including distances, so the map is never the only route to the information. A spatial view is still easier for sighted users.
    - listitem: Flagstone is available in English only at present.
  - heading "Assistive technologies we test with" [level=2]
  - paragraph: VoiceOver on iOS, Dynamic Type at accessibility sizes, Reduce Motion, Dark Mode, and colour-vision simulation for the common forms of colour blindness. Testing is done on physical hardware, not only the simulator.
  - heading "Tell us where we got it wrong" [level=2]
  - paragraph: If something in Flagstone is difficult or impossible for you to use, that’s a bug and we want to hear about it. Please include the device and which assistive technology you were using if you can, but a plain description is completely fine too, and no report is too small.
  - link "Email us about accessibility":
    - /url: mailto:support@skypistudio.com?subject=Flagstone%20accessibility%20feedback
  - paragraph:
    - text: We aim to respond within 3–5 business days. You can also report issues on
    - link "GitHub (opens in new tab)":
      - /url: https://github.com/Skypie99/AccessMap/issues
    - text: ", or use the Feedback option inside the app."
  - paragraph: "Last reviewed: 19 August 2026. We review this statement with each significant release."
- contentinfo:
  - navigation "Site":
    - strong: Flagstone
    - text: "|"
    - link "Support":
      - /url: ../support/
    - text: "|"
    - link "Privacy Policy":
      - /url: ../privacy/
    - text: "| Accessibility |"
    - link "Terms & Community Guidelines":
      - /url: ../terms/
  - paragraph: © 2026 Flagstone. All rights reserved.

      - strong: Photos are optional and described.
      - text: A photo is never the only way information is conveyed.
  - heading "Known gaps" [level=2]
  - paragraph: "We would rather list these than pretend they don’t exist:"
  - list:
    - listitem: Voice Control has not been fully tested (see above).
    - listitem: Photo descriptions are optional, so older reports and reports from people who skipped the field may have no description beyond the barrier’s own text.

  - paragraph: If something in Flagstone is difficult or impossible for you to use, that’s a bug and we want to hear about it. Please include the device and which assistive technology you were using if you can, but a plain description is completely fine too, and no report is too small.

    - link "support@skypistudio.com":

    - text: .

- main:
  - heading "About Flagstone" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Flagstone is a crowdsourced mobile app for mapping accessibility barriers in the real world. Users drop pins at locations where there’s an accessibility issue, such as a missing ramp, a broken sidewalk, or an inaccessible parking spot. The community verifies, resolves, or rejects those reports. The goal is to make cities and neighborhoods easier to navigate for everyone.
  - heading "How to Report a Bug" [level=2]
  - paragraph: If you’ve found something that isn’t working correctly, we’d love to know about it.
  - list:
    - listitem:
      - strong: Email us
      - text: at

        - /url: mailto:support@skypistudio.com
      - text: with a description of what happened and your device/OS version
    - listitem:

        - strong: Open a GitHub issue
        - text: (opens in new tab)
      - text: ": include steps to reproduce, screenshots if possible, and your device type"
  - paragraph: We aim to respond to bug reports within 3–5 business days.

  - heading "How do I report an accessibility barrier?" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Open the app and tap the
    - strong: +
    - text: button (bottom-right of the map screen). Choose the barrier category (ramp, sidewalk, parking, etc.), set the severity, write a short description, and optionally add a photo. Tap
    - strong: Submit
    - text: . Your flag will appear on the map immediately. Other users can then verify or resolve it.
  - heading "How do I delete my account?" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Go to
    - strong: Profile → Settings → Account → Delete Account
    - text: . This permanently deletes your email, display name, all flags you’ve submitted, and all associated photos. This action cannot be undone. If you’d prefer, you can also email us at
    - link "support@skypistudio.com":
      - /url: mailto:support@skypistudio.com
    - text: and we’ll delete it for you within 30 days.
  - heading "Why does the app need my location?" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Flagstone uses your location
    - strong: only while the app is open
    - text: to center the map on where you are and make it easier to place flags at the right spot. We never access your location in the background, and we never store or share your device’s real-time location. When you submit a flag, we only store the specific latitude/longitude you chose for that flag.
  - heading "Are my photos private?" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Photos attached to flags are
    - strong: publicly visible
    - text: on the map, so anyone using Flagstone can see them. Before storing your photo, we automatically strip all EXIF metadata (including GPS coordinates, timestamps, and camera model) so none of that information is ever stored or visible to others.

    - text: "You earn points by contributing to the community:"
    - strong: "+5"
    - text: when a flag you submitted gets verified,
    - strong: "+10"
    - text: when it gets resolved. You also earn
    - strong: "+2"
    - text: for verifying someone else’s flag and
    - strong: "+5"
    - text: for resolving one. Points reflect your community contribution and appear on your profile.

  - paragraph: Yes. Flagstone has a web version that runs in any modern browser. You can view the map without an account. Reporting and verifying flags requires signing in, which works the same way on web as in the mobile app.

  - paragraph: The iOS app is the primary release. An Android version is planned. Check back for updates or join the beta testing program by emailing us.

  - paragraph: We’re happy to assist. Email us and we’ll get back to you within 3–5 business days.

    - text: .

- main:
  - heading "The short version" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Report real barriers honestly. Keep people out of your photos. Don’t post anything hateful, harassing, or deliberately false. Everything can be reported in the app, and reports are reviewed within 24 hours.
  - heading "What Flagstone is." [level=2]
  - paragraph: Flagstone is a community map of accessibility barriers. I’m Sky, and I built it and run it on my own so that disabled people get better information about the places they move through. By using the app, you’re agreeing to these terms.
  - heading "Community-provided information." [level=2]
  - paragraph: Barrier reports come from people like you. I do my best to keep them honest through verification and moderation, but I can’t promise every report is accurate or up to date. Please don’t make Flagstone your only source when your safety is on the line.
  - heading "What you can post." [level=2]
  - paragraph: Real barriers, honestly described. Photos should show the barrier, not people. Please keep faces, licence plates, and anything that identifies a person out of frame.
  - heading "What’s not allowed." [level=2]
  - paragraph: Anything hateful, harassing, sexually explicit, violent, spammy, deliberately false, or that exposes someone’s private information. I remove content that breaks these rules, and I may restrict accounts that post it.
  - heading "Reports and moderation." [level=2]
  - paragraph: Every flag and comment can be reported right in the app. I review reports within 24 hours and take down anything that breaks these guidelines. You can also hide comments on your own device whenever you like.
  - heading "Your content." [level=2]
  - paragraph: What you post stays yours. By posting it, you’re letting Flagstone show it in the app so the community can use it.
  - heading "Your account." [level=2]
  - paragraph: You can delete your account any time from your Profile. Deleting your account permanently removes your profile information, reports and their associated content, direct contributions, feedback, and uploaded photos. This cannot be undone.
  - heading "Changes." [level=2]
  - paragraph: If these terms ever change, the new version will live right here with a new date at the top.
  - heading "Contact." [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Questions or concerns? Reach me at
    - link "support@skypistudio.com":
      - /url: mailto:support@skypistudio.com
    - text: . Flagstone is made in Canada and operates under the laws of British Columbia.

- main:
  - text: Skyler Halisky Technical Support AI-assisted Builder
  - paragraph: For the Runway team
  - heading "Hi, Runway." [level=1]
  - paragraph: I made this while applying for the Consumer Support Specialist role. It is a proof of use, not a reel. I bought a Pro plan on Saturday, gave myself a real assignment instead of a tour, and this is what came out of the weekend.
  - paragraph: "I spend my days in technical support, so I did not just take the tour: I paid attention to where the product created friction, the way a support person can’t help but do. That instinct is the part I would bring to your team: turning what trips up a brand-new user into something support and product can act on."
  - 'figure "Amazon Night Flight 46 seconds first weekend on a Runway Pro plan. Every frame generated in Runway: Gen-4.5, Gen-4 Turbo, Seedance 2.0, and Seedance 2.5, across text-to-video and image-to-video, then upscaled. The input plates were composited in Python, and the reversals, colour match, and assembly were done with ffmpeg, both written with Claude Code. Sound and titling finished in CapCut, once the credits ran out."':
    - text: Your browser cannot play embedded video. The file is at .
    - strong: Amazon Night Flight
    - text: "46 seconds first weekend on a Runway Pro plan. Every frame generated in Runway: Gen-4.5, Gen-4 Turbo, Seedance 2.0, and Seedance 2.5, across text-to-video and image-to-video, then upscaled. The input plates were composited in Python, and the reversals, colour match, and assembly were done with ffmpeg, both written with Claude Code. Sound and titling finished in CapCut, once the credits ran out."
  - heading "How the words got there" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Video models do not spell. So the words are never generated. I built HI RUNWAY and I’M SKYLER by hand into still input plates, using duckweed and plankton sampled from the film’s own frames, then prompted those plates to
    - emphasis: dissolve
    - text: apart and reversed the clips in the edit. What you see assembling was really coming apart.
  - paragraph: "Everything else is straight out of the models: the river, the descent through the canopy, the plunge, the night vision, the burst back into the moonlight."

  - article "Flagstone case study":
    - heading "The problem" [level=2]
    - paragraph: When someone who depends on accessible routes meets a broken ramp or a missing curb cut, reporting it means a municipal form. Describe the problem, submit, wait, hear nothing. Nobody else finds out. There is no way to signal that a barrier is still there, or to confirm that someone fixed it, so one obstacle gets reported by ten people who never learn about each other, and each of them files it from a place they physically go, which is its own disclosure. I met this gap working with the vision loss community. It is the reason for the app.
    - heading "The approach" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: I chose React Native and Expo to force myself to learn cross-platform development while shipping something real. Supabase handled auth and the database so I could focus on the domain problem instead of infrastructure. The pivotal call was implementing
      - link "Postgres Row Level Security (opens in new tab)":
        - /url: https://github.com/Skypie99/AccessMap/tree/main/supabase/migrations
      - text: from day one. Barriers are meant to be seen. A shared map is the whole point, but only the person who filed a report can edit its content; status changes like verifying it or marking it fixed are open to the community that shares the map. That wasn’t an afterthought; it shaped every feature that followed.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The hardest part wasn’t the code. My first designs missed what users actually wanted. They didn’t just want to report problems. They wanted to
      - emphasis: verify
      - text: them, share workarounds, celebrate fixes together. That insight changed everything.
    - paragraph: The map was the other hard part.     - heading "The problem" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Building solo is manageable. Bigger projects are not. When I started coordinating AI agents for more complex work, I hit the same wall every time: without clear decision rights, scope debates never ended. One agent would start building while another assumed we were still in design. No escalation path. No clear lanes. Multi-agent systems need rules, not just good intentions."
    - heading "The approach" [level=2]
    - paragraph: I designed the operating model before I grew the team. A written Constitution sets the authority order (my intent, then the Constitution, then each role’s own file, then its skills), and no agent may amend it. Fifteen roles each own a domain, from product and design through backend, security, QA, accessibility, performance, release, and documentation; a project manager routes decisions to the right lane, and an orchestrator runs the cycles.
    - paragraph: "The rules that matter most are the ones that remove discretion. Every role works on its own branch, never on main, and merging is mine. Database migrations are files with a rollback, never applied changes. No agent sends anything outside the repository, handles a credential, or acts on a privacy-sensitive change without it reaching me first. Exactly one role may message me; the other fourteen write reports I read on my own schedule. A UI change passes a seven-layer design-compile gate before it counts as done. Work that runs unattended is held to a stricter mode still: at most one reversible change per cycle, no external sends, audit-only by default on the products, and one sentinel file that halts all of it."

      - emphasis: see
      - text: it. Who’s active right now? What decisions are waiting on me? Which blocker is about to slip? It all lived in scattered reports and commit logs. I wanted a cockpit.
    - heading "The approach" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "The dashboard reads the team’s own artifacts, the QA reports, decisions, and blockers every role writes, and turns them into an operator’s view: an agent feed, a “What Needs You” ledger of the decisions waiting on me, a blocker board, a health grade per project, and velocity over the last week and month. It is a server-rendered Next.js app. In private use it runs against real state, behind a sign-in that admits exactly one GitHub account, mine."
    - paragraph: "The interesting problem was making any of it public. The real data is sensitive: security findings, private notes, decisions in flight. It can never be published, but a demo nobody can click proves nothing. So there are two builds of one codebase. The public demo runs in a hard-locked demo mode: every data reader short-circuits to a synthetic snapshot before it can touch a real file, every write returns a plausible answer and persists nothing, and a build guard refuses to produce a public build at all unless demo mode is on."
    - paragraph: This demonstrates the support-operations work of making blockers visible, routing decisions, and keeping evidence close to each handoff.
    - heading "What shipped" [level=2]
    - paragraph: A public demo you can drive. Sign in as a guest, approve or defer a decision, triage a blocker, open the command palette, export the reports view as CSV, switch themes. A Think Tank board that sorts ideas into Do it, Later, and Skip, and a dispatch queue with its relay activity. Fifteen agents in the feed and a health grade per project, all on synthetic data that resets each session. The demo says it is a demo, and it dates the snapshot it was built from, so nobody mistakes the numbers for live operations.
    - heading "My role" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Mine.
      - text: The seam. The real data here, including security findings, private notes, and decisions in flight, can never be published, but a demo nobody can click proves nothing. I chose a synthetic snapshot, demo-mode read and write paths, and a build guard. Every data reader short-circuits to a synthetic snapshot before it can reach a real file. The write path is severed, so an approve button returns a plausible answer and persists nothing. And the build itself refuses to produce a deploy until it is told which kind it is, public demo or private real, and refuses a real one outright if the login gate is off.
    - paragraph: The alternative was a single demo-mode flag, which is one misconfigured environment variable away from serving my actual findings to the open internet. These controls cover different points in the path, but they share mode configuration.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The agents’.
      - text: All three layers, and the guard that reads the published snapshot back and fails the build if anything in it looks real.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: What I check.
      - text: That the synthetic build passes its positive checks and refuses unauthorized modes. Those checks verify the tested conditions; they do not establish independent failure tolerance.
    - heading "Reflection" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The build taught me that
      - emphasis: make it public
      - text: and
      - emphasis: keep it private
      - text: aren’t opposites. With the right seam, you can ship a faithful, interactive demo while the sensitive version stays private.

    - heading "The problem" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: I’d been coordinating a small team of AI agents, including a project manager, engineers, a designer, and a security reviewer, across several projects at once. The work was getting done, but I had nowhere to actually
      - emphasis: see
      - text: it. Who’s active right now? What decisions are waiting on me? Which blocker is about to slip? It all lived in scattered reports and commit logs. I wanted a cockpit.
    - heading "The approach" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "The dashboard reads the team’s own artifacts, the QA reports, decisions, and blockers every role writes, and turns them into an operator’s view: an agent feed, a “What Needs You” ledger of the decisions waiting on me, a blocker board, a health grade per project, and velocity over the last week and month. It is a server-rendered Next.js app. In private use it runs against real state, behind a sign-in that admits exactly one GitHub account, mine."
    - paragraph: "The interesting problem was making any of it public. The real data is sensitive: security findings, private notes, decisions in flight. It can never be published, but a demo nobody can click proves nothing. So there are two builds of one codebase. The public demo runs in a hard-locked demo mode: every data reader short-circuits to a synthetic snapshot before it can touch a real file, every write returns a plausible answer and persists nothing, and a build guard refuses to produce a public build at all unless demo mode is on."
    - paragraph: This demonstrates the support-operations work of making blockers visible, routing decisions, and keeping evidence close to each handoff.
    - heading "What shipped" [level=2]
    - paragraph: A public demo you can drive. Sign in as a guest, approve or defer a decision, triage a blocker, open the command palette, export the reports view as CSV, switch themes. A Think Tank board that sorts ideas into Do it, Later, and Skip, and a dispatch queue with its relay activity. Fifteen agents in the feed and a health grade per project, all on synthetic data that resets each session. The demo says it is a demo, and it dates the snapshot it was built from, so nobody mistakes the numbers for live operations.
    - heading "My role" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Mine.
      - text: The seam. The real data here, including security findings, private notes, and decisions in flight, can never be published, but a demo nobody can click proves nothing. I chose a synthetic snapshot, demo-mode read and write paths, and a build guard. Every data reader short-circuits to a synthetic snapshot before it can reach a real file. The write path is severed, so an approve button returns a plausible answer and persists nothing. And the build itself refuses to produce a deploy until it is told which kind it is, public demo or private real, and refuses a real one outright if the login gate is off.
    - paragraph: The alternative was a single demo-mode flag, which is one misconfigured environment variable away from serving my actual findings to the open internet. These controls cover different points in the path, but they share mode configuration.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The agents’.
      - text: All three layers, and the guard that reads the published snapshot back and fails the build if anything in it looks real.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: What I check.
      - text: That the synthetic build passes its positive checks and refuses unauthorized modes. Those checks verify the tested conditions; they do not establish independent failure tolerance.
    - heading "Reflection" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The build taught me that
      - emphasis: make it public
      - text: and
      - emphasis: keep it private
      - text: aren’t opposites. With the right seam, you can ship a faithful, interactive demo while the sensitive version stays private.
    - blockquote: That separation turned out to be the whole design.

  - article "Flagstone case study":
    - heading "The problem" [level=2]
    - paragraph: When someone who depends on accessible routes meets a broken ramp or a missing curb cut, reporting it means a municipal form. Describe the problem, submit, wait, hear nothing. Nobody else finds out. There is no way to signal that a barrier is still there, or to confirm that someone fixed it, so one obstacle gets reported by ten people who never learn about each other, and each of them files it from a place they physically go, which is its own disclosure. I met this gap working with the vision loss community. It is the reason for the app.
    - heading "The approach" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: I chose React Native and Expo to force myself to learn cross-platform development while shipping something real. Supabase handled auth and the database so I could focus on the domain problem instead of infrastructure. The pivotal call was implementing
      - link "Postgres Row Level Security (opens in new tab)":
        - /url: https://github.com/Skypie99/AccessMap/tree/main/supabase/migrations
      - text: from day one. Barriers are meant to be seen. A shared map is the whole point, but only the person who filed a report can edit its content; status changes like verifying it or marking it fixed are open to the community that shares the map. That wasn’t an afterthought; it shaped every feature that followed.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The hardest part wasn’t the code. My first designs missed what users actually wanted. They didn’t just want to report problems. They wanted to
      - emphasis: verify
      - text: them, share workarounds, celebrate fixes together. That insight changed everything.
    - paragraph: The map was the other hard part. To a screen reader a native map is one opaque view, so Flagstone keeps a parallel, linear list of nearby barriers that opens on its own when a screen reader is detected, and selecting a marker no longer drags focus back to the map. Text follows Dynamic Type up through the accessibility sizes, touch targets hold a 44-point floor, contrast is unit-tested against the WCAG ratio, and when Reduce Motion is on the map camera jumps instead of animating. The app is built and tested against WCAG 2.2 AA, with an accessibility check in CI that fails a pull request below its threshold.
    - paragraph: "Privacy set the remaining shape. Location is foreground-only: the app declares no background-location entitlement and calls no background-location API, a line the privacy review held when an unrelated fix tried to add the keys. Every submission, anonymous or signed in, runs the same content filter, and any flag or comment can be reported through the abuse-report sheet Apple requires. Photos are capped in size and scrubbed before upload. Accounts can be deleted, with the cascade handled by a tested pipeline. There is no analytics or tracking SDK in the app."
    - 'figure "Two write paths, not one path with an anonymous flag on it: a signed-in report and an anonymous report reach Postgres through separate code, and Row Level Security enforces both. A flag is a value a later read can forget to check; a second path cannot be entered by accident."':
      - text: Two write paths, not one path with an
      - code: anonymous
      - text: "flag on it: a signed-in report and an anonymous report reach Postgres through separate code, and Row Level Security enforces both. A flag is a value a later read can forget to check; a second path cannot be entered by accident."
    - heading "Where it stands" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A map-first mobile app where accessibility barriers are pinned to real city locations. Report one, verify someone else’s, and follow up when it gets fixed. The
      - link "web build (opens in new tab)":
        - /url: https://flagstone.skypistudio.com
      - text: is browsable today. The iOS app has not shipped. It was submitted to Apple for App Store review on August 31, 2026. Before submission, one early TestFlight build reached a single outside tester. Apple approval and public App Store availability have not been established.
    - paragraph: "Until that review completes there is no adoption to report, and I would rather say so than imply otherwise. What exists is evidence: a test suite in the thousands, with a dated figure receipted below; a real-device simulator walk that produced 48 findings, 46 of them fixed across four waves and 2 deliberately left open as documented scope calls; and a privacy model whose shape, and the reasons for it, follow."
    - heading "My role" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Mine.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Anonymous reporting gets its own write path rather than an
      - code: anonymous
      - text: flag on the shared one. A flag is a value some later code path can forget to read; a second path cannot be entered by accident. The cost is that two paths drift, and they have. I take that trade because drift shows up in review and a missed flag does not.
    - paragraph: "The photo scrubber fails closed: if the location data cannot be verified gone, the upload aborts. The alternative was to carry on with the original bytes, which is what an earlier version silently did. The library call it trusted returns nothing at all, so the “stripped” result was always undefined and the untouched buffer went up. For an app where people photograph places they physically go, a false rejection is an annoyance and a false acceptance is a disclosure."
    - paragraph: The agents’.
    - paragraph: Effectively all of the implementation, the whole test suite, and most of the diagnosis, across more than 1,900 commits. The simulator walk above was theirs too. They found what it found.
    - paragraph: What I check.
    - paragraph: I gate what lands, and I read the failures rather than the summaries. When an audit reports 48 findings, the ones I read first are the ones it closed without a fix, because a process that cannot report a negative is not a process.
    - heading "What went wrong" [level=2]
    - paragraph: A simulator walk found the flag detail sheet’s Report button rendering, looking enabled, taking the tap, and doing nothing. It is the Apple 1.2(b) objectionable-content sheet, and that screen is its only mount point in the whole app, for flags and for comments, so the report mechanism of a product built on things strangers submit was dead in every path, and would have shipped that way.
    - paragraph:
      - text: It had unit tests. They passed. They mounted the sheet on its own, and the defect was in
      - emphasis: where the parent mounted it
      - text: ", which a child’s test cannot see by construction. Four comments in the code asserted the broken arrangement was proven practice, each citing another, and the one citation that pointed outside the ring pointed at a screen where that arrangement is correct for a reason that did not apply here."
    - paragraph: "The structural fix was one line: a closing tag moved from before the pair of sheets to after them. The comments were rewritten as part of the bug, because they were the reason it kept coming back. The repo had already solved this same iOS error twice, and the correct pattern was sitting three lines above the broken one in the same file. The replacement test renders the parent instead of the child, and it was checked the only way that means anything: it fails against the old arrangement."
    - paragraph: "This is the support work Flagstone demonstrates: tracing a failed interaction to its cause, choosing a repair around accessibility and privacy risks, checking the regression evidence, and deciding what is ready to release."
    - heading "Reflection" [level=2]
    - blockquote: "Building this reinforced something I already believed: privacy isn’t a feature you add later. It’s a foundation, especially when the people using your app are sharing vulnerable information about the barriers they face every day."

      - text: "flag on it: a signed-in report and an anonymous report reach Postgres through separate code, and Row Level Security enforces both. A flag is a value a later read can forget to check; a second path cannot be entered by accident."
    - heading "Where it stands" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A map-first mobile app where accessibility barriers are pinned to real city locations. Report one, verify someone else’s, and follow up when it gets fixed. The
      - link "web build (opens in new tab)":
        - /url: https://flagstone.skypistudio.com
      - text: is browsable today. The iOS app has not shipped. It was submitted to Apple for App Store review on August 31, 2026. Before submission, one early TestFlight build reached a single outside tester. Apple approval and public App Store availability have not been established.
    - paragraph: "Until that review completes there is no adoption to report, and I would rather say so than imply otherwise. What exists is evidence: a test suite in the thousands, with a dated figure receipted below; a real-device simulator walk that produced 48 findings, 46 of them fixed across four waves and 2 deliberately left open as documented scope calls; and a privacy model whose shape, and the reasons for it, follow."
    - heading "My role" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Mine.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Anonymous reporting gets its own write path rather than an
      - code: anonymous
      - text: flag on the shared one. A flag is a value some later code path can forget to read; a second path cannot be entered by accident. The cost is that two paths drift, and they have. I take that trade because drift shows up in review and a missed flag does not.
    - paragraph: "The photo scrubber fails closed: if the location data cannot be verified gone, the upload aborts. The alternative was to carry on with the original bytes, which is what an earlier version silently did. The library call it trusted returns nothing at all, so the “stripped” result was always undefined and the untouched buffer went up. For an app where people photograph places they physically go, a false rejection is an annoyance and a false acceptance is a disclosure."
    - paragraph: The agents’.
    - paragraph: Effectively all of the implementation, the whole test suite, and most of the diagnosis, across more than 1,900 commits. The simulator walk above was theirs too. They found what it found.
    - paragraph: What I check.
    - paragraph: I gate what lands, and I read the failures rather than the summaries. When an audit reports 48 findings, the ones I read first are the ones it closed without a fix, because a process that cannot report a negative is not a process.
    - heading "What went wrong" [level=2]
    - paragraph: A simulator walk found the flag detail sheet’s Report button rendering, looking enabled, taking the tap, and doing nothing. It is the Apple 1.2(b) objectionable-content sheet, and that screen is its only mount point in the whole app, for flags and for comments, so the report mechanism of a product built on things strangers submit was dead in every path, and would have shipped that way.
    - paragraph:
      - text: It had unit tests. They passed. They mounted the sheet on its own, and the defect was in
      - emphasis: where the parent mounted it
      - text: ", which a child’s test cannot see by construction. Four comments in the code asserted the broken arrangement was proven practice, each citing another, and the one citation that pointed outside the ring pointed at a screen where that arrangement is correct for a reason that did not apply here."
    - paragraph: "The structural fix was one line: a closing tag moved from before the pair of sheets to after them. The comments were rewritten as part of the bug, because they were the reason it kept coming back. The repo had already solved this same iOS error twice, and the correct pattern was sitting three lines above the broken one in the same file. The replacement test renders the parent instead of the child, and it was checked the only way that means anything: it fails against the old arrangement."
    - paragraph: "This is the support work Flagstone demonstrates: tracing a failed interaction to its cause, choosing a repair around accessibility and privacy risks, checking the regression evidence, and deciding what is ready to release."
    - heading "Reflection" [level=2]
    - blockquote: "Building this reinforced something I already believed: privacy isn’t a feature you add later. It’s a foundation, especially when the people using your app are sharing vulnerable information about the barriers they face every day."

  - article "Ghost Code case study":
    - heading "The problem" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Command-line fluency does not come from reading about commands. It comes from running them, under a little pressure, until your hands know them. I wanted that fluency in the terminal, in Git, and in Claude Code, and studying a list was not getting me there. So instead of only drilling commands, I built the thing I would practise with: a small game I would actually open again. It was my first real build, and it was meant to be."
    - heading "The approach" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "A prompt appears, four command tokens surround the Phantom, and you steer it to the right one. Arcade mode keeps score and takes a spirit for every miss. Learn mode drops the pressure and escalates instead: a hint with the first retry, a second try, then the answer. A card counts as mastered after three correct answers, which is a plain local counter rather than anything adaptive, and cards you have not mastered come up more often."
    - paragraph: The runtime is one HTML file and a deck file. No framework, no build step, no dependencies, no server. That rule meant every feature cost exactly what it weighed, and it kept the whole game readable in one sitting, which is what a practice project needed to be. The reason to build it, the scope of the deck, and that rule were mine; most of the implementation, the deck validator, and the accessibility audits were the agents’, and I played every build.
    - heading "What shipped" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "Fifty-six cards across Claude Code, the macOS terminal, and Git (20, 20, and 16), with a decoy set for each. Keyboard-first play: number keys for the tokens, arrows to move focus, and single keys for the 50/50 lifeline, category, mode, theme, pause, and help. Touch and swipe on phones. Light, dark, and system themes with no flash on load. Progress persists in the browser under one storage key and is never sent anywhere. A GitHub Actions check validates the deck on every push, so a duplicate ID or a decoy that is also the answer cannot land. Built against WCAG 2.2 AA: a live region announces state to screen readers, reduced motion is honoured from the system setting or an in-app toggle, and high-contrast mode is supported."
    - heading "Reflection" [level=2]
    - blockquote: The best constraint I gave myself was “zero dependencies.”
    - paragraph: "It kept a first project the right size, and it set the pattern the later ones follow: ship something small and real, then widen it deliberately."

  - article "Prompt Library case study":
    - heading "The problem" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "A good prompt is a working asset, and mine were being treated as disposable text. The useful ones were scattered across chats, notes, and documents, so finding one meant scrolling, reusing one meant retyping, and improving one meant losing the version before it. I wanted a single place where a prompt could be found in seconds, filled in, run, and refined over time. I set one hard rule for it: no server of mine in the middle."
    - heading "The approach" [level=2]
    - paragraph: The library lives in the browser. Prompts, favorites, run history, and settings sit in localStorage; there is no account and no backend, and the site is a static export. A prompt can carry variables, so one template fills in differently each time, and a versioned JSON import and export moves a library between machines.
    - paragraph: "Running a prompt is the one place data leaves the page, and I made that explicit rather than quiet: the browser sends the prompt and the user’s own Anthropic API key directly to Anthropic over HTTPS, and nothing passes through anything I operate. The client for that call is hand-built rather than an SDK. It streams the reply by parsing server-sent events itself, sorts failures into typed errors (bad key, rate limit, overloaded, network), counts down live when Anthropic asks for a retry, and lets a run be cancelled mid-stream."
    - paragraph: The no-backend rule turned out to be the whole product discipline. There was nowhere to offload a hard decision, so every feature had to be scoped to run on the client and earn its place.
    - heading "What shipped" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Full-text search across the library, categories and tags, favorites, variable fields, per-prompt run history, and Markdown rendering through a small safe-subset parser instead of raw HTML. A choice of Claude models and a max-token setting. Light, dark, and system themes, and a documented set of keyboard shortcuts for search, running, saving, and switching prompts. Built against WCAG 2.2 AA, with screen-reader announcements on copy and run states and reduced motion honoured. Continuous integration runs typecheck, tests, and lint on every pull request, and GitHub Pages deploys from main. MIT licensed.
    - heading "My role" [level=2]
    - paragraph: The product idea and the privacy rule that shaped it were mine, along with the call to build the API client by hand so the only network request in the app is one I can read in full, and the wording that describes that request honestly. The agents wrote most of the implementation and the test suite. I use it for my own prompts, so a broken search or a lost run shows up quickly, and I re-read the one network call every time it changes.
    - heading "Reflection" [level=2]
    - blockquote: "“No server” turned out to be the constraint that kept me honest: every feature had to earn its place with nowhere to offload the hard decisions."
    - paragraph: I built this because my own prompts were scattered everywhere. I would keep the constraint and lose the notes app.

    - paragraph: The no-backend rule turned out to be the whole product discipline. There was nowhere to offload a hard decision, so every feature had to be scoped to run on the client and earn its place.
    - heading "What shipped" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Full-text search across the library, categories and tags, favorites, variable fields, per-prompt run history, and Markdown rendering through a small safe-subset parser instead of raw HTML. A choice of Claude models and a max-token setting. Light, dark, and system themes, and a documented set of keyboard shortcuts for search, running, saving, and switching prompts. Built against WCAG 2.2 AA, with screen-reader announcements on copy and run states and reduced motion honoured. Continuous integration runs typecheck, tests, and lint on every pull request, and GitHub Pages deploys from main. MIT licensed.
    - heading "My role" [level=2]
    - paragraph: The product idea and the privacy rule that shaped it were mine, along with the call to build the API client by hand so the only network request in the app is one I can read in full, and the wording that describes that request honestly. The agents wrote most of the implementation and the test suite. I use it for my own prompts, so a broken search or a lost run shows up quickly, and I re-read the one network call every time it changes.
    - heading "Reflection" [level=2]
    - blockquote: "“No server” turned out to be the constraint that kept me honest: every feature had to earn its place with nowhere to offload the hard decisions."
    - paragraph: I built this because my own prompts were scattered everywhere. I would keep the constraint and lose the notes app.
